text_blocks.snippet: James Watson and Francis Crick discovered the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, relying heavily on crucial X-ray diffraction images produced by Rosalind Franklin and data shared by Maurice Wilkins.
James Watson and Francis Crick: Built the physical 3D model of the double helix at the University of Cambridge and won the 1962 Nobel Prize.
Rosalind Franklin: Captured "Photograph 51," an X-ray diffraction image that revealed the helical dimensions of DNA.
Maurice Wilkins: Directed colleague Franklin's lab and shared her unpublished data with Watson without her knowledge.
Erwin Chargaff: Discovered chemical base-pairing rules (adenine pairs with thymine, cytosine with guanine) that guided Watson and Crick's model. Rosalind Franklin University +5

questions_and_answers.answer: The famous Watson and Crick paper was not a stand alone paper. It was published beside the cryptographic evidence in a second paper. The problem was in 1953 no one thought they were right. The editor of Nature did but there was a lot of diversity of opinion. Linus Pauling thought it was a triple helix for example and his opinion carried a lot of weight. The Nature editor did not ask for it to be peer reviewed as he was happy with the two papers. If it had been the referees might have suggested not publishing it. Roll forward a few years and the double helix is now an accepted fact. Sadly Franklin had died in the interim from cervical cancer and was quietly overlooked. Sexism may well have played a role but being dead didnt help. The weird thing is DNA does not gave a single structure. Whle the bulk is a double helix parts are triple and even quadruple helices.

questions_and_answers.question: The DNA’s ‘double helix’ structure was discovered thanks in part to Rosalind Franklin. Today is her birthday! In 1962, James Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins confirmed the molecular structure of DNA by relying heavily on Franklin’s hypotheses and photographs of DNA strands created with X-ray diffraction. The three men won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the double helix structure of DNA. While Franklin did not win a share of the Nobel Prize despite her essential contributions, her work has not been forgotten.

questions_and_answers.answer: This is a pretty tricky question. I'm not 100% convinced the 1953 discovery of the structure of DNA changed ideas of heredity all that much. The beginning of the 20th century saw the 're-discovery' of Mendel's pea experiments which really boosted the field of genetics. So, by the 1950s scientists had a pretty good idea of how simple genetic inheritance worked, although the physical structure of the genetic material was still a mystery. There was also tension between ideas of evolution; extremely simplified this was Darwinists vs. Lamarckians. So basically they kind of had the idea that there was genetic "stuff" like chromosomes etc, but really until 1953 there was no molecular genetics in the same way there is today. If you are interested in the history of genetics, James Watsons book "The Double Helix" is a fascinating examination of science at the coal-face. questions_and_answers.answer: The woman you're thinking of is, notably, Rosalind Franklin. Her specialty was X-ray crystallography, and she worked with Maurice Wilkins and Raymond Gosling in the early 1950s, continuing their previous work, to apply X-ray diffraction to produce images of DNA. Watson and Crick's models were built and confirmed by data gathered by Franklin, Wilkins and Gosling; the images allowed them to discount previous models and identify the double helix. To say that Rosalind Franklin helped with the experiments is erroneous; she performed the experiments, along with her colleagues (and yes, other work on the problem of structure had been done by other groups around the same time). It would perhaps be more correct to say that Franklin performed the experiments and Watson and Crick interpreted them in more detail (as Franklin's group also came to the conclusion that a double helix was responsible for some of DNA's shape). questions_and_answers.answer: Answer: James Watson and Francis Crick Explanation: The discovery of DNA's structure is one of the most significant breakthroughs in the history of science. James Watson and Francis Crick are credited with discovering the double helix structure of DNA in 1953 at Cambridge University. Their groundbreaking work laid the foundation for modern molecular biology and genetics. However, it's important to understand that Watson and Crick's discovery didn't happen in isolation. They built upon crucial research conducted by other scientists. Rosalind Franklin, a British chemist, played a vital role by using X-ray crystallography to capture detailed images of DNA. Her famous "Photo 51" provided critical evidence about DNA's helical structure and the spacing between its components. Maurice Wilkins, Franklin's colleague at King's College London, also contributed valuable X-ray diffraction data. questions_and_answers.answer: "The correct answer is James Watson and Francis Crick. Key Points The DNA double helix structure was discovered by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953. Their groundbreaking discovery was based on data and insights from several other scientists, including Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, who had conducted X-ray crystallography studies of DNA. Watson and Crick's model of the DNA double helix, along with the complementary base pairing they proposed, laid the foundation for our current understanding of the structure of DNA and its role in genetics. Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962 was awarded to James Watson and Francis Crick."

questions_and_answers.answer: In the 1920's, Linus Pauling studied the brand new technique of X-ray crystallography which came into use for determining the arrangement of atoms in a crystal. In particular, Pauling deduced rules of interpreting X-ray diffraction images and used the technique to discover the helical substructure of several globular proteins, including hemoglobin. He proposed that DNA would have a triple helix structure. In 1949, Erwin Chargaff made very precise determinations of the percentages of each base (A, C, G, and T) in DNA isolated from cells of a variety of organisms. He demonstrated that two rules always held. The first was that the total amount of purine bases (A and G) equaled 50% as did the amount of pyrimidine bases (C and T). He also discovered that the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of G equals the amount of C.
